output.title: Skin-irritation / adhesion-lift tag cluster — current vs prior window
output.summary: The leading hypothesis attributes the adhesion_flag and skin-irritation feedback increase to the known high-motion + elevated-skin-temperature adhesive-lift mechanism (KI-AD-007). A direct check of the mechanism's own driver variables is a valid falsifying test: motion_intensity was essentially unchanged between prior and current windows and skin_temp_delta_c actually declined, so neither driver increased in the direction the mechanism requires even as adhesion_flag rose. This does not confirm a new firmware- or lot-specific defect (regional breakdown is fairly uniform and the firmware rate ratio interval includes one), but it does undercut the specific causal story offered, leaving the finding correlational and the status unresolved rather than confirmed as a continuation of the known mechanism.

leading_hypothesis.statement: The skin-irritation/adhesion feedback cluster and the rise in adhesion_flag rate are consistent with the already-open, unresolved adhesive-lift mechanism (high motion intensity combined with elevated patch-site temperature delta) rather than a new firmware- or lot-specific defect.

alternative_hypotheses.statement: The rise in adhesion_flag rate reflects a lot-specific or otherwise localized hardware/reporting change unrelated to the motion-intensity-plus-skin-temperature mechanism described in KI-AD-007, since neither driver variable (motion_intensity, skin_temp_delta_c) moved in the direction the mechanism requires.
alternative_hypotheses.falsifying_test: If motion_intensity had risen materially alongside the adhesion_flag increase, that would support the stated mechanism; instead motion_intensity was essentially flat between windows ({f_1} vs {f_2} for adhesion_flag rose while motion_intensity moved only marginally), and skin_temp_delta_c fell. This absence of co-movement in both purported drivers is inconsistent with a driver-linked explanation and instead supports an alternative (lot/sensor/regional) cause.

deterministic_findings.label: adhesion_flag rate ratio, firmware 1.4.0 vs 1.4.2, current window

supporting_evidence.claim: Adhesion_flag telemetry rate increased from {f_2} to {f_1} between prior and current windows.
Skin-irritation-tagged feedback record count increased from {f_6} to {f_5} between prior and current windows, with sampled text describing patch lift during high-intensity or sweaty sessions.

The knowledge base documents an open, unresolved adhesive-lift mechanism tied to high motion intensity plus elevated skin temperature delta (KI-AD-007), and explicitly instructs support staff not to close such tickets as an expected characteristic.

A prior adhesive lot recall (INC-2025-031) was a confirmed hardware incident, showing that adhesion clusters can sometimes reflect a genuine lot-specific defect rather than the general open mechanism.

counter_evidence.claim: Skin_temp_delta_c telemetry rate actually decreased from {f_4} to {f_3}, which does not support an intensifying thermal driver behind the reports.

The adhesion_flag rate ratio between firmware 1.4.0 and 1.4.2 in the current window is {f_7}, with a confidence interval that includes one, so there is no firmware-specific signal distinguishing this cluster from baseline.

Motion_intensity telemetry was nearly flat between prior and current windows (rate 50.91 to 51.67 intensity_per_device_day), showing no material increase in the motion-intensity driver that the leading hypothesis says underlies the adhesion_flag rise.

Adhesion_flag rate breakdown by region in the current window is fairly uniform across benelux, dach, iberia, nordics, and uk (all clustered near 0.12-0.15 flags_per_device_day), which does not show a concentrated regional spike that would be expected if a distinct lot or regional defect were driving the increase, but also does not confirm the generic motion+temp mechanism since motion_intensity itself did not rise.

knowledge_sources.section: KI-UK-008 UK gym sweat lift (open, regional flavour of KI-AD-007)

Continue logging adhesion and skin-irritation tags per the support playbook and escalate any tightening cluster (e.g., regional or lot concentration) to operations rather than closing tickets as expected.

Regional breakdown of adhesion_flag is fairly uniform, so it neither confirms a distinct lot/regional defect nor strongly confirms a generic wear mechanism; per-device or per-lot identifiers are not available through these tools.

output.title: Rising claims-interpretation ticket cluster: wellness score misread as clinical result
output.summary: The leading hypothesis attributes the claims-interpretation spike entirely to communications/misreading, explicitly declining to examine telemetry because KD-05 frames the score as separate from hardware signals. However, the pack's own finding that a large share of these tickets are co-tagged data-accuracy was not verified against ticket content: a follow-up search for accuracy-complaint language in current-window data-accuracy tickets returned no matches, leaving the co-tag overlap unexplained. This does not confirm a scoring/sensor defect, but it means the alternative explanation (a real data-accuracy issue contributing to the same ticket cluster) has not been excluded, so status is downgraded from CONFIRMED to UNCERTAIN pending a check of whether data-accuracy co-tagged tickets describe factual inconsistency in the score rather than clinical misinterpretation.

leading_hypothesis.statement: Wearers are interpreting the on-screen readiness score as a clinical or diagnostic result rather than a wellness indication, a communications/claims-risk pattern matching KD-03 and KD-05 and recurring in the same shape as INC-2025-002.

alternative_hypotheses.statement: A subset of the claims-interpretation cluster reflects a genuine data-accuracy problem (e.g., a sensor or scoring-input drift affecting skin-temperature or motion inputs to the readiness score) rather than pure misreading of a correct wellness score, since a large fraction of these tickets are co-tagged data-accuracy.
alternative_hypotheses.falsifying_test: Pull the sampled data-accuracy co-tagged tickets and check whether they describe the score as numerically inconsistent, jumping, or contradicting other readings (an accuracy complaint) rather than describing it as a clinical/diagnostic result; if a substantial share describe factual inconsistency in the score rather than a clinical misread, the pure-communications hypothesis is falsified for that subset.

supporting_evidence.claim: Sampled current-window tickets describe the readiness score being read as a health verdict, lab result, or clinical finding rather than a wellness indication.

KD-03 defines a dedicated claims-misread intake queue with symptoms matching these tickets (treating the number as a clinical result, asking about disease, cancelling plans, forwarding screenshots) and tags it claims-interpretation, often alongside data-accuracy.
KD-05 is the policy register governing what can be claimed about the readiness score, and staff must cite it (not a live ticket) as the rule source for claims-risk flags.

A prior incident (INC-2025-002) with an identical ticket shape was closed as a confirmed communications incident, not a device incident, with the explicit lesson that a claims-shaped ticket cluster can be real risk without being a sensor defect.

KD-05 explicitly states that hardware telemetry (battery, radio, adhesion) is not a health claim and does not become one under wellness classification, decoupling this cluster from a hardware investigation.

counter_evidence.claim: A large share of current tickets are also tagged data-accuracy, which could suggest wearers perceive the score itself as wrong rather than purely misreading its meaning; this was not ruled out with telemetry in this investigation.

A targeted search for current-window tickets tagged data-accuracy describing the score as wrong or inaccurate returned no matching records, which is inconsistent with the pack's claim that a large fraction of the claims-interpretation cluster ({f_3}) is co-tagged data-accuracy in a way that has already been ruled out as unrelated to accuracy; the co-tag overlap remains unexplained rather than confirmed as pure misreading.

knowledge_sources.section: INC-2025-002 — Readiness screenshots as clinical results (comms)

recommended_actions.description: Route the current claims-interpretation ticket cluster to Communications/Legal for review against KD-05, following the same closure template used for INC-2025-002, rather than opening a hardware or scoring-algorithm investigation.
Have Communications review current on-screen copy near the readiness score (per KD-03 staff script) to determine whether a copy bug is contributing to the misread, and file a copy-bug ticket if so.
Do not issue any wearer-facing clinical confirmation or denial; continue using the KD-03 staff script for support responses.

uncertainty: Whether a specific UI copy change or app or firmware release is concentrating this cluster was not tested; the sample spans multiple app and firmware versions.
The overlap with data-accuracy tags was not further decomposed to rule out a contributing (even if minor) scoring-accuracy issue alongside the interpretation issue.
Only a small sample per window was inspected in detail; full ticket text for the remaining current-window records was not reviewed.

Whether the data-accuracy co-tag on current-window claims-interpretation tickets reflects genuine score/sensor inconsistency versus simply co-occurring language was not resolved; a direct query for accuracy-complaint language returned no matches, leaving the overlap unexplained.

No telemetry inputs to the readiness score (e.g., skin_temp_delta_c, motion_intensity) were compared across the current versus prior window for the specific cohort/region driving the ticket spike, so a real scoring-input anomaly coinciding with the ticket rise cannot yet be excluded.

The falsifying test (checking whether data-accuracy co-tagged tickets describe factual score inconsistency rather than clinical misinterpretation) has not been completed with a definitive sample; absence of matches so far does not confirm or refute either hypothesis.

output.title: Overheating-tagged support tickets trace to known cosmetic battery-UI issue, not device thermal events
output.summary: The falsifying test for the leading hypothesis is to isolate overheating-tagged tickets lacking battery/app-ui co-tags and check for genuine thermal-event language; finding such a subset in meaningful numbers would falsify the pure mislabeling explanation. A first pass search for this exact pattern (device hot to touch, unrelated to charging or UI) returned no matching records in the current window, consistent with the existing hypothesis, but the test remains the correct falsifying check and should be repeated with a larger sample and across the prior window before treating the mislabeling explanation as fully settled.

leading_hypothesis.statement: Tickets tagged 'overheating' are a mislabeling of the known cosmetic app-UI issue (harsh red battery chrome, KI-UI-011) combined with the Nordics cold-weather battery-drain regional offset, not evidence of actual device or skin overheating.

alternative_hypotheses.statement: A genuine device-level thermal event is occurring in a subset of overheating-tagged tickets that do not co-occur with battery or app-ui tags, and this subset is being masked by aggregating with the much larger cosmetic/UI-driven cluster.
alternative_hypotheses.falsifying_test: Pull the subset of overheating-tagged tickets that do NOT also carry battery or app-ui tags and check whether their text describes genuine device/skin heat (e.g., 'hot to touch', 'burning', localized skin heat unrelated to charging or screen color) rather than cold-weather drain or red UI. If such a non-overlapping subset exists in meaningful numbers with genuine thermal language, the mislabeling hypothesis is falsified for that subset.

supporting_evidence.claim: In current and prior windows, essentially every overheating-tagged ticket also carries battery and app-ui tags, and sampled text describes cold-weather drain and a warm-feeling phone or alarming sync screen rather than a hot wearable.
The known issues register documents KI-UI-011, a standing accepted cosmetic defect where app battery chrome uses a harsh red fill below a low battery threshold that reads as an overheating warning.

The knowledge base explicitly warns against using skin_temp_delta_c to construct a temperature narrative, noting its correlation with battery_drain_pct is close to zero and that it is a patch-site delta, not ambient or core temperature.
A prior closed incident describing Nordics winter drain tickets was resolved as not an incident and accepted as a stable regional battery characteristic rather than a defect.

counter_evidence.claim: The candidate signal itself is flagged safety-adjacent with a low band and falling trend, and the rate ratio confidence interval does not exclude one, indicating triage code did not find a strong statistical anomaly to begin with.

A targeted search for overheating-tagged records describing genuine device/skin heat independent of battery-UI or charging context returned zero matching records in the current window, which is consistent with (not contradictory to) the mislabeling hypothesis but was the specific falsifying check attempted.

knowledge_sources.section: KI-UI-011 App battery chrome reads as "overheating" (standing, cosmetic)

recommended_actions.description: Retag or relabel these support tickets from overheating to battery with a note pointing to KI-UI-011 so the safety-adjacent tag stops firing on cosmetic UI complaints.

No production or customer-facing action warranted; continue tracking the existing Nordics battery-drain offset under its own standing known-issue entry rather than reopening as an overheating investigation.

uncertainty: Sampled feedback is a small subset of the matched records in each window and may not capture every overheating-tagged ticket; a subset could in principle describe genuine thermal discomfort rather than UI or battery confusion, though the tag co-occurrence pattern strongly suggests otherwise.

No version-axis comparison of skin_temp_delta_c was run, so a narrow firmware- or app-specific thermal regression masked within the flat aggregate cannot be fully excluded, though nothing in the gathered evidence points toward one.

pre_critic.title: Overheating-tagged support tickets trace to known cosmetic battery-UI issue, not device thermal events
pre_critic.summary: The overheating tag cluster (affected users and prior events per the triage record; falling trend, rate-ratio confidence interval does not exclude one) does not correspond to a device thermal defect. Feedback text sampled from both windows shows the same repeating pattern: users describe cold-weather battery drain and a warm phone during sync or a red, alarming battery UI, and the overheating tag co-occurs almost universally with battery and app-ui tags (see {f_3}, {f_4}, {f_5}, {f_6}). Telemetry on skin_temp_delta_c (a patch-site delta, not ambient or core temperature) is flat to falling between windows (see {f_1}, {f_2}), and the known-issues register explicitly documents KI-UI-011: app battery chrome renders a harsh red fill below a low-charge threshold that reads as an overheating warning, and states that skin_temp_delta_c must not be used to construct a temperature story, since its correlation with battery_drain_pct is near zero. The real, checkable phenomenon behind these tickets is the Nordics regional battery-drain offset (KI-NW-014 / INC-2024-088), previously closed as not an incident.

leading_hypothesis.statement: Tickets tagged 'overheating' are a mislabeling of the known cosmetic app-UI issue (harsh red battery chrome, KI-UI-011) combined with the Nordics cold-weather battery-drain regional offset, not evidence of actual device or skin overheating.

alternative_hypotheses.statement: Skin temperature delta rises meaningfully alongside these reports, indicating a real thermal event at the patch site.
alternative_hypotheses.falsifying_test: Compare skin_temp_delta_c current vs prior window rate; already checked and delta declined slightly, and the knowledge register reports near-zero correlation with battery_drain_pct, so this hypothesis is not supported.

alternative_hypotheses.statement: A firmware or app version change introduced a genuine overheating regression in the current window.
alternative_hypotheses.falsifying_test: Run compare_versions on skin_temp_delta_c or adhesion_flag by firmware_version or app_version across current vs prior windows; not run here because feedback text and known-issue documentation already point to a UI or labeling explanation rather than a version-specific thermal regression, and the trend is falling, not rising.

The known issues register documents KI-UI-011, a standing accepted cosmetic defect where app battery chrome uses a harsh red fill below a low battery threshold that reads as an overheating warning.

A prior closed incident describing Nordics winter drain tickets was resolved as not an incident and accepted as a stable regional battery characteristic rather than a defect.
